items.followUp: What is the habitat of the Marco Polo sheep, and what feature is it especially known for?

rubric.why: Identifies its characteristic habitat and a notable feature.
rubric.description: Names the Pamir Mountains and its large horns.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both the habitat and the horn feature.

rubric.why: Shows what kind of animal it is and the origin of its name.
rubric.description: Identifies it as a wild sheep (argali) associated with the explorer Marco Polo.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the animal and its association with Marco Polo.

modelAnswer: The Marco Polo sheep is a large wild sheep, or argali, found in the Pamir Mountains of Central Asia.
It is named after Marco Polo and is especially known for its large, spiralling horns.

items.followUp: Differentiate between homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids.

rubric.why: Defines sister chromatids by their origin and relationship.
rubric.description: Sister chromatids are identical copies of one chromosome joined at the centromere.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as identical copies of the same chromosome, joined at the centromere.

rubric.why: Distinguishes non-sister chromatids as belonging to homologous chromosomes.
rubric.description: Non-sister chromatids belong to a pair of homologous chromosomes, one inherited from each parent; they may exchange segments during crossing over.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying their homologous chromosomes and distinguishing them from sister chromatids.

modelAnswer: Sister chromatids are identical copies of one chromosome joined together at the centromere.
Non-sister chromatids belong to the two homologous chromosomes, one from each parent; they are not identical copies and may exchange segments during crossing over.

items.followUp: Write the full forms of ATP and ADP.

rubric.why: Checks the correct expansion of FADH₂.
rubric.description: Expands FAD as flavin adenine dinucleotide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct full form.

rubric.why: Checks the correct expansion of NADH.
rubric.description: Expands NAD as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct full form.

modelAnswer: FADH₂ stands for flavin adenine dinucleotide (in its reduced form).
NADH stands for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (in its reduced form).

items.followUp: Name three factors that can affect the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Identifies a major factor affecting photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Names light intensity as a limiting factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming light or light intensity.

rubric.description: Names at least one other limiting factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration, temperature, water, or chlorophyll.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming any one additional valid factor.

modelAnswer: The main limiting factors of photosynthesis include light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature.
Water availability and the amount of chlorophyll can also limit the rate of photosynthesis.

items.followUp: What is the active site of an enzyme?

rubric.why: Identifies the two substances and the site involved in the complex.
rubric.description: The enzyme-substrate complex forms when a substrate binds to an enzyme's active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the binding of the substrate to the enzyme's active site.

rubric.why: Shows that the complex is a temporary intermediate in enzyme action.
rubric.description: The complex is temporary and forms during the enzyme-catalysed reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the complex is temporary or naming it correctly.

modelAnswer: An enzyme-substrate complex is the temporary combination formed when a substrate binds to the active site of its specific enzyme.
The complex forms during the enzyme-catalysed reaction and then breaks apart as products are released.

items.followUp: Why does amylase act on starch but not on proteins?

rubric.why: Recognises that pepsin acts specifically on protein.
rubric.description: Pepsin is specific for proteins, which are present in meat.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying protein as pepsin's substrate and explaining its specificity.

rubric.why: Explains the enzyme action or the products of protein digestion.
rubric.description: Pepsin's active site binds protein and breaks it into smaller peptides.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the active site to protein digestion or naming smaller peptide products.

modelAnswer: Pepsin is specific in its action: its active site binds protein, the nutrient present in meat.
It digests the protein into smaller peptides; it does not digest carbohydrates or fats.

items.followUp: Which nutrient supplies most of the body's immediate energy, and why?

rubric.why: Recognises that a healthy diet requires a range of food components.
rubric.description: States that all food components are important and should be included in a balanced diet.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for recognising the importance of a balanced diet or the necessity of all components.

rubric.why: Gives a valid reason for the usefulness of a food component.
rubric.description: Identifies a component and a valid function, such as proteins for growth and repair or carbohydrates for energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a food component and correctly stating its function.

modelAnswer: All components of food are important, so a balanced diet is most useful.
Proteins are especially useful for growth and repair of body tissues, while carbohydrates provide energy.

items.followUp: What is translocation in plants, and which tissue carries out this process?

rubric.why: Defines the source as the region producing food for transport.
rubric.description: A source, usually a mature leaf, produces sugars by photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the source as a food-producing part of the plant.

rubric.why: Defines the sink as a region that uses or stores transported food.
rubric.description: A sink, such as a root, fruit or growing region, uses or stores the food; phloem transports it from source to sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a sink and its role in receiving, using or storing food.

modelAnswer: A source is a plant part, usually a mature leaf, that produces sugars by photosynthesis.
A sink is a part that uses or stores those sugars, such as a growing region, root or fruit.
The source-and-sink relationship enables food to be transported through the phloem to parts of the plant where it is needed.
